extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, anthropologists, evolutionary biologists, and readers interested in species/race classification
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evidential criteria for deciding whether human races (or closely-allied forms) should be ranked as distinct species, sub-species, or merely varieties; and factors influencing the extinction or decline of human races. Focus is on morphological, reproductive, distributional, and historical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual fertility of intercrossed races
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the races, when intercrossed, produce perfectly fertile offspring (mutual fertility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that 'the perfect fertility of the intercrossed races of man, if established, would not absolutely preclude us from ranking them as distinct species.' He also cautions that domestication tends to eliminate sterility which commonly results from crossing species in nature, and that complete sterility can be incidental to unknown differences in reproductive constitution. Thus mutual fertility is an important test but not an absolute proof of specific identity; exceptions and modifying factors (e.g. domestication, sterility affecting germen only) must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenotype of hybrid offspring
rubrics_metrics.description: The characters presented by offspring from a cross (whether blended/intermediate or closely like one parent) as evidence for parent-forms being species or varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues no general rule can be trusted: 'The ordinary result of a cross is the production of a blended or intermediate form; but in certain cases some of the offspring take closely after one parent-form, and some after the other.' He cites examples (e.g. African crosses producing wholly black or white offspring, versus intermediate mulattoes in America) and warns this variability in hybrid outcomes weakens reliance on this criterion alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic distribution and enormous range
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the distribution and range of the forms accords with that of other undoubtedly distinct species (e.g., wide or disjoint ranges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin states the 'enormous range of man' would influence a naturalist towards treating races as distinct species, and that the distribution of races accords with that of other distinct mammal species. Geographic separation and distinct ranges can be used as supporting evidence for specific distinction, but must be weighed with other criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coexistence without fusion (absence of fusion when mingled)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether different forms, when mingled together in large numbers in the same country, keep distinct or fuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasises this as 'the usual and best test of specific distinctness': if forms inhabit the same area without fusing, that supports species status. He gives counterexamples (Brazil, Chiloe, Fiji, Polynesia) where extensive mingling leads to blended populations, arguing against treating such groups as distinct species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy vs variability of distinguishing characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether characters that supposedly distinguish a race are constant across individuals and time, or highly variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that 'distinctive characters of all the races were highly variable' and that 'it may be doubted whether any character can be named which is distinctive of a race and is constant.' He warns naturalists that defining species based on inconstant characters is rash, and points to examples (negro slaves in Brazil, Polynesians, Hottentot women) where variation undermines supposed distinguishing traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduation/continuous variation between forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether forms 'graduate into each other' by innumerable intermediate steps (continuous variation) independent of intercrossing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin considers this among the most weighty arguments against treating races as distinct species: extensive gradation implies they are varieties of a single species. He recounts the long history of differing judgments by naturalists (from one up to sixty-three races) to illustrate that gradation makes fixed boundaries arbitrary. He also compares analogous cases in other genera where naturalists unite forms that graduate into one species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of term: species vs sub-species vs race
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing appropriate taxonomic rank/term (species, sub-species, race) to express degree of difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin suggests the term 'sub-species' might be appropriately applied to forms that possess many characteristics of true species but hardly deserve full species rank, while acknowledging that 'race' may continue in common use. He emphasises the desirability of using the same terms for the same degrees of difference but cautions this is rarely possible across diverse genera and sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerous minor resemblances in structure and mental faculties as evidence of common descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement in many small, unimportant structural details and in mental traits between forms supports descent from a common progenitor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues it is 'extremely improbable' that numerous trivial resemblances would have been independently acquired, so their presence is strong evidence for common ancestry and thus for classifying forms under a single species. He cites examples of shared habits, gestures, and simple technologies across human races as reinforcing this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence vs common descent (caution interpreting superficial similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishing whether similar traits are due to convergence (independent evolution toward a similar form) or shared descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin acknowledges convergence occurs (analogy like whale and fish) but cautions it is 'extremely rash' to attribute close similarity in many structural points to convergence among widely distinct ancestors. He notes cases (domestic pigs descended from two species) where traces of distinct ancestry remain in skull bones, implying that careful anatomical evidence (e.g., skeletal details) can reveal true relationships despite superficial convergences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestication effects on sterility and character convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestication can reduce sterility between crossed forms and induce convergence of appearance among breeds descended from distinct stocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin observes that domestication 'tends to eliminate the sterility which is so general a result of the crossing of species in a state of nature' and gives examples (improved breeds of pigs, cattle) where selecting for similar traits produced convergent external appearance despite descent from different species; internal skeletal traces may still reveal distinct origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes and indicators of extinction or decline of races
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors and observable signs that lead to partial or complete extinction of races (competition, decreased fertility, disease, changed habits, wars, infant mortality, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin lists many proximate causes: competition between tribes/races; periodic famines; nomadic habits; prolonged suckling; wars; accidents; sickness; licentiousness; stealing of women; infanticide; especially lessened fertility and high child mortality. He emphasises that contact with civilized nations often accelerates decline via new diseases, vices (e.g., spirituous liquors), changed habits, and psychological effects (loss of motives). He uses historical examples (Tasmanians, Maories, Sandwich Islands/Hawaiians) and demographic data to show decreased fertility and high mortality among children as particularly potent causes. These factors serve as criteria for diagnosing causes of population decline.
